lead.headline: Winter Games brings snow and ice to the Commodore
lead.dek: Epyx turns the home computer into a seven-event winter arena, with October reviewers cheering from the sidelines.
body: Epyx is taking its sporting competition into colder country. Winter Games, reviewed for the Commodore 64 in October’s Computer Entertainer, offers a winter counterpart to Summer Games and Summer Games II. The newsletter gives it four out of four for both graphics and play value. This is a game on the current month’s review desk, not a claim of a release on a particular day this week.

The original Commodore manual sets out seven events: Ski Jump, Bobsled, Figure Skating, Free Skating, Hot Dog Aerials, Speed Skating and Biathlon. That range shifts the contest between ice, snow and the air above the slope. These are the computer edition’s events, not a roster borrowed from a later console version.

Epyx’s title history describes solo competition or as many as eight people taking turns. A home-computer sports evening can therefore be a shared contest without eight machines or a connection to an online service. The joystick and the next attempt remain the center of attention.

For a fall software shelf, the appeal is variety within one sporting package. October’s enthusiastic review gives Commodore owners a concrete title to investigate as winter approaches; it does not establish a national sales ranking. The competition here is on the screen, with no later commercial totals smuggled onto the scoreboard.

stories.headline: GEnie courts the home-computer caller
body: General Electric is bringing its information-services resources to home-computer owners through GEnie. The online-history timeline dates the announcement to October 21; a later ANALOG review also identifies that date in its account of the service’s beginnings. Dial-up information and entertainment are the proposition for personal-computer callers.

The recorded launch rates are $35 per hour in prime time and $5 per hour in evenings and on weekends. Those are hourly charges, not a monthly subscription. The historical account gives 300- and 1200-bps access with the same off-peak rate, a useful distinction for callers comparing modem speed against the connect-time bill.

The announcement date should not be confused with an undisputed first day of operation: another period retrospective gives October 1 for going online. October 21 is the announcement peg here. Later signup fees and later speed surcharges are not part of this launch account.

stories.headline: Atari puts a mouse-driven desktop below $1,000
body: October’s COMPUTE! hands-on report finds the Atari 520ST becoming widely available after its January announcement. The reviewed system combines 512K of memory with an 8-MHz Motorola 68000, a two-button mouse and GEM’s icons, windows and drop-down menus.

The editorial prices are $799 for a monochrome system and $999 for an RGB system. The adjacent advertisement gives $999.95 for its color-monitor bundle, plus shipping and applicable taxes. These are published package quotations, not a survey of completed street transactions.

MIDI, RS-232 and parallel interfaces broaden the machine’s uses. Early systems load TOS from disk; Logo is shipping, while BASIC was unfinished when the reporter wrote. The report’s future storage plans and prototypes should not be mistaken for accessories already on the counter.

stories.headline: Nintendo keeps its New York experiment local
body: Computer Entertainer’s October report describes a limited mid-October Nintendo release in the New York City area. That opening precedes this issue’s week: it is a continuing regional experiment, not a new nationwide console launch.

The contemporary package quotation is $159.95 suggested retail for the control deck, two controllers, R.O.B. with Gyromite, and the Zapper with Duck Hunt. The newsletter names area retailers including Crazy Eddie’s, J&R Music and Toys-R-Us.

A national release in early 1986 remains an expectation in that report. The immediate story is a robot, a light gun and a carefully bounded retail test, with the rest of the country still waiting for a broader rollout.

briefs.headline: King’s Quest II reaches the review desk
briefs.summary: COMPUTE! describes 93 animated screens and a $49.95 IBM PC/PCjr edition requiring 128K, a disk drive and color monitor. Apple II development is still under way.

briefs.headline: Hacker is a fictional online mystery
briefs.summary: Activision’s game dispenses with instructions in October’s demonstration report. Its simulated computer mystery is not a live network intrusion.

briefs.headline: A hard disk takes an expansion slot
briefs.summary: Plus Development’s 10MB Hardcard carries its disk and controller on a PC expansion board at $1,095 list. InfoWorld’s October 21 review is bibliographically verified; no review verdict is quoted.

periodAd.headline: A faster line for the bulletin-board evening
periodAd.summary: Courier 2400: $695 list in October COMPUTE! The internal Cermetek Infomate 1200-TPC is a different, 1200-bps proposition at $198.
periodAd.tagline: Period buying desk; editorial reconstruction, not a quoted advertisement.

market.headline: Connect time is part of the computer budget
market.summary: GEnie’s recorded $5-per-hour evening/weekend launch rate competes for the home caller. October COMPUTE! quotes The Source at $10.80 per nonprime hour at 1200 bps, with a further $1.20 for 2400 bps. Rates and speeds must be compared together.

worldAnchor.headline: Reagan addresses the United Nations on its fortieth anniversary
worldAnchor.summary: On October 24, President Reagan addressed the United Nations on its fortieth anniversary, discussing regional conflicts and his forthcoming meeting with Mikhail Gorbachev. The Geneva meeting is still ahead.

bbsNote.headline: 2400 bps gets cheaper while GEnie seeks home callers
bbsNote.summary: October’s COMPUTE! reports modem price cuts and a U.S. Robotics program for heavily used bulletin boards. The following are reported desk notes, not recovered historical posts.

posts.text: Arlan R. Levitan reports that U.S. Robotics is working with bulletin-board system operators and offering a special acquisition deal to operators of heavily used boards to promote 2400-bps access. No specific board names or numeric sysop discount are supplied.
2400-bps access was added in August. October reporting gives the prime/nonprime supplements as $1.80/$1.20 over the 1200-bps hourly rates; this is month-level coverage, not a new October 21 event.
Courier 2400 list price is $695; Cermetek’s internal Infomate 1200-TPC is $198. These are different speeds and products, not interchangeable quotations.

curiosity.headline: Atari’s terminal menu skips the fashionable speed
curiosity.summary: A contemporary columnist found 2400 bps missing from an Atari ST terminal-accessory menu.
curiosity.detail: In COMPUTE! October p.108, Arlan R. Levitan describes an ST demonstration whose terminal-emulator configuration offered 300, 1200, 4800 and 9600 bps but omitted 2400. He asked, “What happened to 2400?” The anecdote concerns that demonstrated configuration, not a claim that the ST serial hardware cannot support 2400 bps.

gadgetWatch.headline: Canon’s VM-E1 combines camera and 8mm recorder
gadgetWatch.summary: Canon’s October introduction combines camera and 8mm recorder in one unit at 298,000 yen in its manufacturer history. The VM-E1 has a monochrome viewfinder and an 8.5–51mm lens; a US on-sale date is not established.

items: GEnie: October 21 announcement/start is supported by Nieman and the March 1987 ANALOG review, but other period retrospectives say October 1 for operation. A contemporary launch dispatch was not recovered. Treat exact operational day as unresolved; rates are corroborated retrospectively.

InfoWorld October 21 p.45 metadata and review title are verified, but Google Books returned no readable review image; detailed Hardcard claims remain secondary-source verified, and no review quotation is supplied.

Computer Entertainer full PDF download was blocked by HTTP 403 / web open size limit. Its indexed Nintendo p.13 text and indexed Winter Games review details were readable; no fabricated further review details or game prices added.
Gaming stories are same-month pegs, not exact-week release announcements. No new milestone is asserted for this week.

Underground scene reporting recovered in detail is dated November 21 and looks back to October 15. Its later reporting must not become a fictional current-week dispatch. No independently read October 19 NYT text was obtained.
Games are an editorial shelf selection, not sales rankings. Music uses Billboard Top Rock Tracks dated October 26; movies use the October 25-27 domestic weekend.
Detailed underground coverage dated November 21 is omitted rather than backdated.
